question: What made you want to study meteorology?
lookingFor: Genuine personal motivation tied to a real interest in atmospheric science, not just liking weather.

bullets: Name a specific moment or experience that sparked the interest
Connect it to what you actually enjoy about the science, not just watching weather
Show it's grown into something sustained, not a passing curiosity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I grew up in a part of the country that gets serious thunderstorms every summer, and I used to sit on the porch timing the gap between lightning and thunder just to guess how close the storm was. That childhood habit turned into genuine curiosity about why storms form where they do, and by the time I was doing my A-levels I was reading synoptic charts for fun before checking if school was cancelled. What keeps me hooked now is the physics underneath it all, how a few basic laws of fluid motion and thermodynamics can produce something as violent and beautiful as a supercell.

commonMistakes: Saying I've always loved weather with nothing concrete behind it
Describing enthusiasm for extreme weather without any interest in the underlying science
Making it sound like a hobby rather than an academic pursuit
followUps: What part of the science behind that interests you most?

question: Why do you want to study meteorology here specifically, rather than at another university?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course's structure, staff, or facilities, not generic praise.

bullets: Reference a specific module, forecasting lab, or research group
Explain why that specific feature matters to your goals
Show you compared it against alternatives, not just applied broadly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at a few programs and yours stood out because the second year includes a dedicated synoptic forecasting practical where you issue real forecasts and get scored against verification data, which most courses only offer as an optional add-on later. I also read some of Dr. Ahmed's work on convective storm initiation, and that's the exact area I got interested in after a school project on flash flooding. Compared to other courses I looked at, this one gets you hands-on with real data earlier, and that matches how I learn best.

commonMistakes: Praising the university's reputation without mentioning the course content
Giving an answer that would apply equally to any meteorology program
Naming a professor or module without explaining why it matters to you
followUps: What would you want to get out of that practical specifically?

question: Do you remember the first time you found weather genuinely fascinating?
lookingFor: A concrete, personal anecdote that shows authentic long-standing curiosity.

bullets: Describe a specific, real memory rather than a generic one
Explain what specifically struck you about it
Link it briefly to how your interest has developed since
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was about nine when a hailstorm hit in the middle of a heatwave and completely confused me, because I couldn't understand how ice could fall from a sky that hot. I asked my dad and he didn't know either, so I looked it up myself and found out about updrafts carrying hailstones up and down inside a storm cloud until they got too heavy to stay aloft. That was the first time I remember thinking science could explain something that felt almost magical, and I've been chasing that feeling ever since.

commonMistakes: Inventing a story that sounds rehearsed rather than genuine
Describing the memory without explaining why it mattered
Skipping straight to present-day interests with no origin story at all
followUps: How has your understanding of that event changed since then?

question: Have you read or followed anything outside the school curriculum that deepened your interest in meteorology?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine self-directed engagement with the subject beyond what's required.

bullets: Name something specific: a book, forecasting model output, blog, or podcast
Explain a specific idea from it that stuck with you
Show it changed how you think about the subject, not just that you consumed it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following the ECMWF's ensemble forecast charts for the past year, mostly because a physics teacher showed us how spread between ensemble members tells you how confident a forecast actually is, and I found that idea of quantifying uncertainty fascinating. I also read Andrew Blum's book on the hidden infrastructure behind weather forecasting, which made me realise how much of meteorology is really about data collection and computing, not just watching clouds. It's shifted my interest from just wanting to know what the weather will be to wanting to understand how we know.

commonMistakes: Naming a source vaguely without any specific detail from it
Listing several sources with no depth on any of them
Confusing weather apps with genuine wider reading
followUps: What's one thing from that reading you'd want to learn more about here?

question: Have you done any hands-on work related to meteorology, like building a weather station, coding, or a school project?
lookingFor: Real, described experience that demonstrates initiative and technical engagement with the subject.

bullets: Describe what you actually built, measured, or analysed
Mention a specific technical challenge you had to solve
Explain what you learned that you couldn't have got from a textbook
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For my extended project I built a small weather station with a Raspberry Pi and some cheap sensors, and logged temperature, humidity, and pressure for about four months. The hardest part was actually the pressure sensor drifting over time, so I had to calibrate it against the nearest official station's readings, which taught me a lot about why real observation networks care so much about instrument standards. Comparing my little dataset to the forecast each day also made me appreciate how much local microclimate effects can throw off even a good regional forecast.

commonMistakes: Describing a project vaguely with no technical specifics
Overstating the scale or sophistication of what was actually done
Not being able to explain what went wrong or what was learned
followUps: What would you do differently if you built it again?

subtopic: Awareness of maths and physics demands
question: Meteorology is a maths and physics heavy degree. How prepared do you feel for that, and why do you want to take it on?
lookingFor: Realistic self-assessment of the quantitative demands, backed by genuine willingness and some evidence of aptitude.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly what the degree actually demands mathematically
Point to specific coursework or experience that shows you can handle it
Explain why you want that rigor rather than a softer alternative
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know the degree leans heavily on calculus, differential equations, and fluid dynamics, and honestly that's part of why I want to do it rather than a more general earth science course. I've taken further maths alongside physics and found the mechanics modules the ones I enjoyed most, particularly anything involving rates of change. I'd rather struggle through the maths that actually explains atmospheric behaviour than study weather in a way that stays qualitative, because I want to understand the mechanism, not just describe it.

commonMistakes: Downplaying or being unaware of how quantitative the degree is
Claiming confidence with no evidence from actual coursework
Suggesting you'd prefer to avoid the maths if possible
followUps: Which area of maths do you find hardest, and how do you work at it?

question: Is there a recent weather event you followed closely? Talk us through it.
lookingFor: Current awareness of meteorology in the news, with some understanding of the science behind the event, not just headlines.

bullets: Name a specific, real event with rough timing or location
Explain what was meteorologically interesting about it, not just its impact
Show some understanding of why it happened or was forecast the way it was
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I followed the flooding in parts of the UK last autumn quite closely, partly because it happened near family. What struck me was how the forecasters had flagged the risk of a slow moving low pressure system days in advance, but the actual rainfall totals still surprised people because the system stalled for longer than the models expected. It made me appreciate the gap between knowing roughly what's coming and knowing exactly how bad it will be, which seems to be one of the harder problems in operational forecasting.

commonMistakes: Only describing the human impact with no meteorological detail
Picking an event you clearly don't know much about
Getting basic facts about the event wrong
followUps: What do you think made that event particularly hard to forecast?

question: How would you explain the difference between weather and climate to someone with no science background?
lookingFor: A clear, correct distinction stated simply, showing genuine conceptual understanding rather than a memorised line.

bullets: State that weather is short-term atmospheric conditions and climate is the long-term average pattern
Use a simple, correct analogy or example
Avoid conflating a single event with a climate trend
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Weather is what's happening in the atmosphere right now or over the next few days, like whether it's raining today or how windy it'll be this weekend. Climate is the average pattern of that weather over a much longer period, usually decades, so it's more like the typical range you'd expect for a place in a given month. I like the analogy that weather is your mood on a given day, while climate is more like your personality over years, one cold day doesn't say anything about climate any more than one grumpy morning says something about someone's character.

commonMistakes: Using the terms interchangeably by accident during the answer
Claiming a single extreme event proves or disproves a climate trend
Giving a definition with no example to make it concrete
followUps: Why do people sometimes confuse the two?

question: Meteorology leads to quite different careers, forecasting, research, aviation, broadcasting. Do you have a direction in mind?
lookingFor: A genuine, informed sense of direction that's specific enough to be credible but open to change.

bullets: Name a specific area and explain what draws you to it
Show you understand roughly what that career actually involves
Stay open to the course changing your mind rather than sounding fixed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to operational forecasting, ideally somewhere like aviation meteorology, because I like the idea of decisions actually depending on my forecast within hours rather than years. I spent a day shadowing at a regional airport and saw how much pressure there is to get low visibility calls right, which was intense but exactly the kind of applied, high stakes work I want. That said, I know a lot of people go in with one idea and come out interested in research instead, so I'm keeping an open mind once I actually get into the atmospheric dynamics modules.

commonMistakes: Having no direction at all and seeming disengaged from the field's actual career paths
Naming a career with no understanding of what it involves day to day
Sounding so fixed on one path that you seem inflexible
followUps: What's drawn you to that path specifically, rather than the alternatives?

question: What do you think a professional meteorologist actually does day to day, beyond presenting the forecast on TV?
lookingFor: Realistic understanding that most meteorology work is technical and behind the scenes, not on-camera.

bullets: Show awareness that broadcasting is a small fraction of the field
Describe realistic day to day tasks like model interpretation, data quality checks, or writing forecasts
Demonstrate you're drawn to the actual work, not the public-facing image
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Most meteorologists never appear on camera at all. A lot of the job is interpreting output from several different numerical models that often disagree with each other, deciding which one is likely closer to right given the current situation, and then writing that judgement up as a forecast for a specific audience, whether that's the public, an airline, or a shipping company. There's also a lot of unglamorous work checking observation data for errors before it even goes into a model. That's actually the part that appeals to me, the judgement call in the middle of conflicting information.

commonMistakes: Assuming the job is mostly presenting on television
Describing the job in vague terms without any real day to day detail
Showing no awareness that forecasting involves interpreting model disagreement
followUps: Why does that appeal to you more than the broadcasting side?

question: In simple terms, what actually causes wind?
lookingFor: Correct core physics, pressure gradient force driving air from high to low pressure, stated clearly.

bullets: Identify the pressure gradient force as the fundamental driver
Explain that air moves from high pressure toward low pressure
Mention that other factors like the Coriolis effect and friction then shape the direction and speed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Wind happens because air moves from areas of higher pressure toward areas of lower pressure, trying to even things out, and the bigger that pressure difference is over a given distance, the stronger the wind. That basic push is called the pressure gradient force. It doesn't just blow in a straight line from high to low though, because the Earth's rotation bends the path through the Coriolis effect, and friction near the ground slows it down and changes the angle further.

commonMistakes: Saying wind is just caused by temperature without connecting it to pressure differences
Leaving out the pressure gradient force entirely
Describing the Coriolis effect as the primary cause of wind rather than something that deflects it
followUps: Why does wind near the surface not blow directly from high to low pressure?

question: Why does rising air cool, even if it doesn't lose heat to its surroundings?
lookingFor: Understanding of adiabatic cooling, the link between pressure, volume, and temperature as a parcel rises.

bullets: Explain that pressure decreases with altitude
Connect that to the parcel expanding as it rises
Explain that expansion does work on the surroundings, which uses up internal energy and cools the parcel
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As a parcel of air rises, it moves into an environment of lower pressure, so it expands. That expansion means the parcel is doing work pushing against the surrounding air, and since no heat is being added or removed, that energy has to come from somewhere, which is the parcel's own internal energy. As the internal energy drops, so does the temperature, which is why we call it adiabatic cooling, it's not about losing heat to the surroundings, it's about the parcel expending its own energy to expand.

commonMistakes: Explaining it as simply it's colder higher up without the mechanism
Confusing adiabatic cooling with the parcel losing heat to the air around it
Not connecting pressure decrease with altitude to the expansion
followUps: What happens to the cooling rate once condensation starts?

question: Can you explain, in basic terms, how a cloud forms?
lookingFor: Correct sequence involving air rising, cooling, reaching saturation, and condensing onto nuclei.

bullets: Explain that air needs to rise and cool to reach its dew point
Mention condensation nuclei as necessary for water vapour to condense onto
Describe the result as tiny water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A cloud forms when air rises, expands, and cools until it reaches its dew point, the temperature at which it's holding as much water vapour as it can. Beyond that point the water vapour starts condensing, but it needs something to condense onto, tiny particles like dust, pollen, or sea salt called condensation nuclei. Once that happens you get billions of tiny water droplets or, if it's cold enough, ice crystals, all suspended together, and that's what we see as a cloud.

commonMistakes: Skipping the role of condensation nuclei entirely
Confusing dew point with a fixed temperature rather than something dependent on humidity
Describing clouds as made of water vapour rather than condensed liquid or ice
followUps: Why do clouds have flat bases?

question: What is the Coriolis effect, and how does it influence weather systems?
lookingFor: Understanding that it's an apparent deflection caused by Earth's rotation, and its practical effect on wind direction in different hemispheres.

bullets: Explain it as an apparent deflection caused by the Earth rotating beneath moving air
State the direction of deflection differs by hemisphere, right in the Northern, left in the Southern
Connect it to why large scale wind systems curve rather than flowing straight from high to low pressure
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The Coriolis effect is an apparent deflection of moving air caused by the fact that the Earth is rotating underneath it, so from our point of view on the surface, the air seems to curve even though it's really travelling in a straight line relative to space. In the Northern Hemisphere that deflection is to the right of the direction of motion, and in the Southern Hemisphere it's to the left. It's why large scale systems like cyclones spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern, and why wind around a low pressure system curves inward rather than blowing straight into the centre.

commonMistakes: Claiming the Coriolis effect is what makes water spin down a drain a particular way, a common myth at that small scale
Getting the hemisphere directions backwards
Describing it as a real force rather than an apparent effect of the rotating reference frame
followUps: Why is the Coriolis effect negligible for something small like a draining sink?

question: What's the difference between a warm front and a cold front?
lookingFor: Correct basic distinction in structure, slope, and typical weather associated with each.

bullets: Define a front as the boundary between two air masses of different temperature
Explain that cold fronts are steeper and move faster, often bringing sharper, shorter bursts of weather
Explain that warm fronts are shallower and slower, bringing more prolonged, gradual weather ahead of them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Both are boundaries between a warmer and a colder air mass, but they behave differently depending on which one is advancing. A cold front is where cold air is pushing under warm air, and because cold air is denser it wedges in quite steeply, which is why cold fronts tend to move fast and bring short, intense bursts of rain or thunderstorms as they pass. A warm front is where warm air is advancing over cold air, and it slides up over it on a much shallower slope, so you tend to get a longer period of gradually thickening cloud and steadier rain well ahead of the front itself.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which front is associated with the steeper slope
Describing fronts without mentioning the air masses on either side
Assuming both fronts bring the same type of weather
followUps: What would you expect to see on a barometer as a cold front passes?

question: What actually causes the seasons? A lot of people get this wrong, what's the real explanation?
lookingFor: Correct explanation based on axial tilt, not distance from the sun.

bullets: Correctly identify the Earth's axial tilt, not orbital distance, as the cause
Explain how tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight received through the year
Note that hemispheres experience opposite seasons at the same time as a result
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's not actually about how close the Earth is to the sun, a common misconception, it's about the Earth's axial tilt of about twenty three and a half degrees. As the Earth orbits, that tilt means different hemispheres are angled more directly toward the sun at different times of year, so they get more direct, concentrated sunlight and longer days, which is summer, while the other hemisphere gets more oblique, spread out sunlight and shorter days, which is winter. That's also why the two hemispheres are always in opposite seasons at the same time.

commonMistakes: Attributing seasons to the Earth being physically closer to the sun in summer
Failing to mention axial tilt at all
Not connecting the explanation to why hemispheres have opposite seasons
followUps: Why is Earth actually closest to the sun in early January, and why doesn't that make the Northern Hemisphere hottest then?

question: Can you explain how the greenhouse effect works?
lookingFor: Correct mechanism involving incoming shortwave and outgoing longwave radiation, and the role of greenhouse gases.

bullets: Explain that the sun's energy arrives mostly as shortwave radiation that passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface
Explain that the surface re-emits energy as longwave infrared radiation
Explain that greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some of that longwave radiation, trapping heat rather than letting it all escape to space
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sunlight arrives as shortwave radiation, and most of it passes through the atmosphere fairly easily and warms the Earth's surface. The surface then re-radiates that energy back out, but as longwave infrared radiation because it's much cooler than the sun. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and water vapour are good at absorbing that longwave radiation, and they re-emit it in all directions, including back down toward the surface, which keeps some of that heat from escaping straight to space. Without any greenhouse effect at all the planet would actually be far too cold to support life as we know it, so the natural effect itself isn't the problem, it's the amount we've added to it.

commonMistakes: Describing the atmosphere as a physical barrier or blanket without mentioning radiation wavelengths
Implying the greenhouse effect is entirely artificial or bad, missing that a natural version keeps Earth habitable
Confusing shortwave and longwave radiation
followUps: Why is water vapour actually the most abundant greenhouse gas, and why don't we talk about controlling it directly?

question: Walk me through what has to happen for a raindrop to actually form and fall.
lookingFor: Correct sequence from evaporation through condensation to droplet growth and precipitation.

bullets: Start with evaporation putting water vapour into the air
Describe condensation around nuclei forming tiny cloud droplets
Explain droplets need to grow large and heavy enough, through collision and coalescence or ice processes, to overcome updrafts and fall
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It starts with evaporation, usually from the ocean, putting water vapour into the air. That moist air eventually rises, cools, and condenses into tiny cloud droplets around condensation nuclei, but those droplets on their own are far too small and light to fall, they'd just float. For rain to actually happen, those droplets need to collide and merge with each other, a process called collision and coalescence, or in colder clouds ice crystals grow by picking up water vapour more efficiently than the surrounding droplets. Either way, the droplets or crystals need to get heavy enough that gravity beats the updraft holding them up, and then they fall as precipitation.

commonMistakes: Stopping at cloud formation without explaining how droplets grow large enough to fall
Assuming all clouds automatically produce rain
Leaving out the role of updrafts in keeping small droplets suspended
followUps: Why do some clouds never produce rain?

question: What tools or instruments do meteorologists actually use to observe the atmosphere?
lookingFor: Awareness of the range of observation systems beyond a simple thermometer, and roughly what each measures.

bullets: Name at least two or three distinct tools, such as radar, satellites, and radiosondes
Briefly describe what each one actually measures or detects
Show awareness that forecasting relies on combining many observation types, not just one
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Weather radar sends out pulses and measures what bounces back off precipitation, which is how we see the shape and intensity of storms in something close to real time. Satellites give us the bigger picture from above, tracking cloud cover, storm systems, and even sea surface temperatures over huge areas. Then there are radiosondes, weather balloons carrying sensors that measure temperature, humidity, and pressure as they rise through the atmosphere, which is really important because it gives us a vertical profile, not just a surface reading. Forecasters combine all of that with surface stations and ocean buoys to build a full picture before it even gets near a model.

commonMistakes: Naming only a thermometer or barometer with no awareness of radar or satellites
Confusing what radar and satellites each actually detect
Not mentioning that observations feed into forecast models
followUps: Why is a vertical profile of the atmosphere important, not just surface readings?

question: Why do weather forecasts get less reliable the further ahead they try to predict, even with powerful computers?
lookingFor: Understanding of chaos theory and sensitivity to initial conditions, not just computers aren't good enough yet.

bullets: Explain that the atmosphere is a chaotic system sensitive to tiny errors in initial conditions
Note that observation data always has some small uncertainty or gaps, which grows over time in the model
Mention ensemble forecasting as the practical response to this uncertainty
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's not really a computing power problem, it's more fundamental than that. The atmosphere is a chaotic system, which means tiny differences in the starting conditions, differences too small for us to even measure precisely, can lead to completely different outcomes a week or two later, an idea sometimes called the butterfly effect. Since our observation network can never capture the atmosphere's exact state everywhere at once, every forecast starts with some small uncertainty, and that uncertainty compounds the further out you run the model. That's why forecasters now run ensembles, dozens of slightly varied simulations, so they can show a range of possible outcomes and how confident they actually are, rather than pretending a single run is exact.

commonMistakes: Blaming the limitation purely on insufficient computing power or bad models
Not mentioning sensitivity to initial conditions or chaos theory at all
Suggesting forecasts could become perfectly accurate indefinitely into the future with enough improvement
followUps: What does an ensemble forecast actually tell you that a single deterministic run doesn't?

question: What is El Nino, and why does it matter to weather patterns far from the Pacific?
lookingFor: Basic understanding of ENSO as an ocean-atmosphere coupling with far reaching effects, teleconnections.

bullets: Describe El Nino as a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific
Explain that it's tied to changes in trade winds and ocean circulation, not an isolated ocean event
Mention teleconnections, how it shifts weather patterns in distant regions like altering jet stream position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: El Nino is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific, and it happens alongside a weakening of the usual trade winds that push warm water westward. Because the ocean and atmosphere are so tightly linked in that region, that shift in ocean temperature changes where thunderstorm activity and rising air are concentrated, which then reshapes atmospheric circulation patterns like the jet stream on a much larger scale. That's why El Nino can influence rainfall and temperature patterns as far away as North America or even parts of Africa, through what are called teleconnections, even though the actual warming is happening thousands of miles away in the Pacific.

commonMistakes: Describing El Nino as purely an ocean phenomenon with no atmospheric component
Not being able to explain why it affects weather in distant regions
Confusing El Nino with a single storm or short term event rather than a multi-month to multi-year pattern
followUps: What's La Nina, and how does it differ?

question: What is the jet stream, and why do meteorologists care about it so much?
lookingFor: Correct description of the jet stream and its role in steering weather systems.

bullets: Describe it as a narrow band of strong winds high in the atmosphere, formed by temperature contrasts between air masses
Explain that it roughly separates cold polar air from warmer air toward the equator
Explain its importance in steering surface weather systems and influencing how fast or slow they move
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The jet stream is a narrow band of very fast moving winds several miles up in the atmosphere, usually near where the tropopause sits, and it forms because of the sharp temperature contrast between cold polar air and warmer air further toward the equator. It tends to mark the rough boundary between those two air masses, and its position shifts throughout the year as that temperature contrast changes with the seasons. Meteorologists care about it so much because it effectively steers surface weather systems, a dip or ridge in the jet stream can pull a storm further south or hold it in place for days, which is often the difference between a quick passing system and a prolonged spell of extreme weather.

commonMistakes: Confusing the jet stream with surface level wind
Not connecting it to temperature contrasts between air masses
Missing its role in steering and influencing the speed of surface weather systems
followUps: What happens to surface weather when the jet stream becomes unusually wavy or blocked?

question: What conditions does a tropical cyclone need in order to form and strengthen?
lookingFor: Knowledge of the key ingredients, warm ocean water, moisture, low wind shear, and background rotation.

bullets: Warm ocean water to a sufficient depth, generally cited around 26 to 27 degrees Celsius, to fuel the storm with heat and moisture
Low vertical wind shear, so the storm's structure isn't torn apart as it develops
Enough distance from the equator for the Coriolis effect to provide the initial spin, plus some pre-existing disturbance to organise around
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A tropical cyclone needs warm ocean water, usually at least around twenty six or twenty seven degrees Celsius down to a reasonable depth, because that heat and moisture is essentially the storm's fuel supply, evaporating and condensing to release latent heat that drives the whole system. It also needs low vertical wind shear, meaning wind speed and direction don't change too much with height, because strong shear tears the developing storm's structure apart before it can organise. And it needs enough distance from the equator for the Coriolis effect to actually give the system spin, which is why you almost never see tropical cyclones form right on the equator itself, plus usually some existing disturbance like a tropical wave to act as a seed for the circulation to build around.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning warm water and ignoring wind shear or the Coriolis requirement
Claiming hurricanes can form directly on the equator
Describing the storm's energy source vaguely without mentioning latent heat release
followUps: Why do hurricanes weaken quickly once they move over land or cooler water?

question: What is atmospheric pressure, and how do we actually measure it?
lookingFor: Correct definition tied to the weight of air above a point, and a basic grasp of how it's measured and why it changes with altitude.

bullets: Define atmospheric pressure as the weight of the column of air above a given point
Mention a barometer as the instrument used to measure it
Explain that pressure decreases with altitude because there's less air above you higher up
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Atmospheric pressure is essentially the weight of all the air sitting above a given point, pressing down on everything below it. We measure it with a barometer, and the units you'll usually see on a weather chart are hectopascals or millibars, they're the same thing under different names. Pressure decreases as you go up in altitude, because the higher you are, the less air is left above you to weigh down on that point, which is also part of why it gets harder to breathe at high altitude, there's simply less air, and less oxygen, pressing in around you.

commonMistakes: Defining pressure vaguely as just how heavy the air is without the column concept
Not knowing the instrument used to measure it
Getting the direction of change with altitude backwards
followUps: Why do meteorologists often adjust pressure readings to sea level before comparing stations at different altitudes?

question: In broad terms, how does a computer actually go about predicting the weather?
lookingFor: Basic conceptual grasp of numerical weather prediction, initial conditions plus physical equations solved forward in time.

bullets: Explain that models start from a snapshot of current observed conditions across a grid covering the atmosphere
Explain that the model applies the physical equations governing fluid motion and thermodynamics to step that state forward in time
Note the trade-off between grid resolution, computing power, and how far ahead or how detailed the forecast can be
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A numerical weather model starts by taking a snapshot of the current state of the atmosphere, temperature, pressure, humidity, wind, gathered from observations and spread across a three dimensional grid covering the region or the whole globe. From there it applies the physical equations that govern how fluids and heat behave, things like the equations of motion and thermodynamics, and solves them step by step forward in time, essentially calculating what the atmosphere at each grid point should look like a few minutes later, then using that as the new starting point for the next step. The catch is that finer grid spacing gives a more detailed and often more accurate forecast, but it costs enormously more computing power, which is why global models tend to use coarser grids than the small regional models used for things like severe storm forecasting.

commonMistakes: Describing forecasting as pattern matching against historical weather rather than solving physical equations
Not mentioning that the model needs an accurate starting snapshot of current conditions
Missing the trade-off between resolution and computational cost
followUps: Why might a coarser global model miss a severe thunderstorm that a finer regional model catches?
